how-to-calculate-freight-class.html.text:
← LTL freight class estimator

How do I calculate LTL freight class?

Every LTL quote form asks for a class before it will give you a price, and the number is not arbitrary: for most freight it comes straight out of density — total weight divided by total cubic feet. Work out the density and you know the band. The part that catches small shippers is that density is measured to the outside of the packaging, pallet included, so the box decides the class as much as the product does.

Open the free freight class estimator

The arithmetic, in order

  1. Multiply length × width × height in inches, then divide by 1728. That is cubic feet for one piece.
  2. Multiply by the number of pieces for total cube, and multiply the per-piece weight by the same count for total weight.
  3. Divide total weight by total cube. That is density, in pounds per cubic foot.
  4. Read the band. 50 lb/ft³ and above is class 50; the bands step up through class 500 as density drops below 0.5 lb/ft³.

Worked example

A single pallet measuring 48 × 40 × 36 inches at 500 lb is 40.00 cubic feet, giving a density of 12.5 lb/ft³ and an estimated class 85. The next lower band, class 77.5, starts at 13.5 lb/ft³ — so it is within reach two ways: add about 40 lb to the same footprint, or take the cube down to roughly 37 cubic feet, which is about three inches off the pallet height. Neither is obvious from the weight and the class number alone, which is why the estimator shows the cube, the density, and the distance to the next band together.

Common questions

How do I calculate LTL freight class?

Multiply length by width by height in inches and divide by 1728 to get cubic feet per piece, then multiply by the number of pieces for total cube. Divide total weight by total cube to get density in pounds per cubic foot. That density falls into a class band: 50 lb/ft3 and above is class 50, and the bands step up through class 500 as density falls below 0.5 lb/ft3. Density is the input you control; carrier rules, stowability, handling, and liability can still change the class the carrier actually bills.

Why is my freight class higher than I expected?

Almost always because the shipment is lighter for its size than you assumed — class rises as density falls. Packaging is usually the cause: an oversized carton, a tall pallet with empty headspace, or dunnage that adds cube without adding weight. The cube is measured to the outside of the packaging, including the pallet, not to the product inside it.

Can I lower my freight class by changing the packaging?

Sometimes, and it is worth checking before you book. Because density is weight divided by cube, you can raise density either by consolidating more weight onto the same footprint or by removing cube that carries no weight — trimming pallet height, using a smaller carton, or stacking rather than shipping two half-full pallets. The estimator shows the density the next lower class band needs, so you can see whether the gap is inches or out of reach.

Is a density estimate the same as the class the carrier bills?

No. Density gives you the class band to expect and to sanity-check a quote against, which is what makes the carrier's form answerable. The billed class can still differ: many commodities have a fixed class regardless of density, and carriers can reclassify on stowability, handling, or liability, or re-measure the shipment at the terminal. Treat the estimate as preparation for the quote, not a substitute for it.

Common questions

Why does density decide the class rather than weight?

Because a trailer runs out of space long before it runs out of weight. A carrier is selling floor and cube, so the question that sets the rate is how much weight your freight brings per cubic foot it occupies. Density is total weight divided by total cube, and the class bands here run from class 50 at 50 lb/ft³ and up, down to class 500 below 0.5 lb/ft³. Light, bulky freight is expensive to move for exactly the reason it feels cheap to lift.

How close am I to the next class down?

The estimate answers it in inches and pounds rather than in density, because nobody ships a lb/ft³. The worked example is a single 48″ × 40″ × 36″ pallet at 500 lb: 40 ft³, 12.5 lb/ft³, class 85. The next band down, class 77.5, starts at 13.5 lb/ft³, and the page states what that costs you on the dock — pack the same 500 lb to 33.3″ instead of 36″, or leave the height alone and put 540 lb on the pallet. Those are the only two levers in the formula: the footprint is the pallet and the weight is the goods, so height and load are what a shipper can actually move. Sometimes 2.7 inches is a strap pulled tighter. Sometimes it is not available, and it is worth knowing that before you quote rather than after.

How much taller can the pallet get before it costs me a class?

The estimate states that too, and it is the number that catches people out. Class is set by the dimensions the carrier measures, not the ones on your bill of lading, and a dimensioner reading two inches of stretch wrap you did not count re-rates the shipment after it has shipped. The worked example above has 1.5″ of headroom: at 500 lb on a 48″ × 40″ footprint, anything over 37.5″ falls out of class 85 and into 92.5. When that clearance is under half an inch the page says the freight is on the band line instead of quoting a headroom figure, because at that point a tape measure and a dimensioner disagreeing is enough to change the bill.

Which dimensions do I measure?

The packed outside dimensions, including the pallet, the stretch wrap, and anything that overhangs. Not the box, not the product. A carrier dimensioner measures the space your freight actually occupies on the trailer, so measuring the carton and ignoring a 2-inch overhang is how an estimate and a re-class notice end up disagreeing. Height is measured from the floor, pallet included.

Is weight per piece or for the whole shipment?

Per piece — and pieces means identical ones. The estimate multiplies both cube and weight by the piece count, so density is unchanged by how many identical pallets you ship. That is correct for density, and it is also why a mixed shipment cannot be estimated in one pass here: if your pallets differ, run the heavy configuration and the light one separately, because the real shipment classes as its parts rather than its average.

Why isn’t this an official freight class?

Because density is only one of the four things that set an NMFC classification. Handling, stowability, and liability — how fragile, how stackable, how valuable and how prone to theft or damage — can move the class regardless of how dense the freight is, and many commodities have their own NMFC item number that is not density-based at all. This is a planning estimate for the density half. Verify it with your carrier or a qualified freight professional before booking, and expect accessorials (liftgate, residential, inside delivery) to sit on top of whatever the class turns out to be.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the estimate runs entirely in your browser. Nothing about your freight is sent anywhere. The usage counter is a local, opt-out tally of which features were used, never your dimensions or weights.

Are my numbers saved, and can I share them?

Your last entry is saved in this browser's local storage, so refreshing the page or coming back later restores it — nothing is uploaded. “Copy shareable link” puts the same dimensions, weight, and piece count in the page's URL fragment (after the #) instead, so sending that link to a broker or coworker opens this page with the exact same freight estimated, without either of you retyping anything. A link takes priority over a saved draft when you open one.

vs-looking-up-the-class-table-yourself.h.text:
← LTL Freight Class Estimator

This calculator vs. looking up the class table yourself

The 18-row density-to-class table is public and looking a known density up in it by hand works fine. What tends to go wrong is upstream of the table: converting inches to cubic feet, multiplying by piece count, and finding the right row without an off-by-one on a boundary.

What each approach actually does

Looking it up yourself means converting the outside dimensions to cubic feet (length × width × height in inches, divided by 1728), multiplying by piece count for the whole shipment, dividing total weight by total cube to get density, and then scanning an 18-row table for the band that density falls into. None of those steps is hard individually. Getting all four right, in order, without a unit slip or an off-by-one on a boundary density, is where a hand calculation most often drifts from the right class.

This calculator does the same conversion and lookup with nothing to get wrong in between: enter outside dimensions, weight, and piece count, and it returns the cube, the density, and the class band in one step. It also rearranges the density formula for height to answer two questions the table alone does not: how much shorter this pallet would need to be packed to reach the next class down, and how much headroom is left before a carrier's dimensioner re-rates it into the class above.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is the density-to-class table itself public information?Yes — both approaches use the same 18-row band table.
Did I convert inches to cubic feet correctly, and multiply by the right piece count?This calculator — those two steps are where a hand calculation is most likely to drift.
How much shorter would this pallet need to be packed to reach the next class down?This calculator's repack-height figure, not a manual rearrangement of the density formula.
How much headroom is there before a carrier's dimensioner re-rates this pallet into the class above?This calculator — the same estimate states the clearance directly.
I already have the density calculated and just need the class band.Either — a one-line table lookup and this calculator will agree.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't the density-to-class table public? Why not just look it up myself?

The 18-row density band table is not a secret, and looking up a known density in it by hand works fine. Where a hand calculation tends to go wrong is upstream of the table: converting outside dimensions in inches to cubic feet (dividing by 1728, not 12), multiplying by piece count correctly for the whole shipment rather than one piece, and then finding the right row without an off-by-one on a boundary density. This calculator does the conversion and the lookup in one step, so there is nothing to get wrong between typing in the dimensions and reading the class.

What does this calculator do that the table alone doesn't?

Past the class lookup, it states the two numbers a shipper can actually act on: how much shorter the pallet would need to be packed to reach the next class down, and how much headroom is left before a carrier's dimensioner re-rates it into the class above. Neither of those is in the table itself — they require rearranging the density formula for height, which is exactly the kind of algebra a quick manual lookup skips.

When is looking it up by hand the better choice?

When you already have the density calculated and just need to check which of the 18 bands it falls in — that's a one-line table lookup and typing it into a calculator may not save real time. This calculator earns its keep when the density still has to be computed from raw dimensions and piece count, and especially when you want the repack and re-class headroom numbers the table alone doesn't give you.

vs-smc3-fastclass.html.text:
← LTL Freight Class Estimator

This calculator vs. SMC³ FastClass

Two different starting points: FastClass looks up the exact NMFC item for a commodity you can already name. This page estimates the density-based class band for a pallet you have not classified yet — the input FastClass needs before it can answer anything.

What each tool is for

FastClass, from SMC³, is a licensed software product — installed or accessed online — built on the official National Motor Freight Classification (NMFC) data. Its job is exact-item lookup: given a commodity, it returns the NMFC item number, the class or classes that apply, and the packaging, sub-group, and rule notes that go with it, described on SMC³'s own FastClass product page. It is sold as an ongoing licence to carriers, logistics providers, and shippers, and it is the closest thing the LTL industry has to an authoritative classification lookup for a commodity you can already name.

This calculator does not have a commodity database and does not look up an NMFC item — that is not the job it does. It estimates the density-based class band from the outside dimensions, weight, and piece count of a pallet or crate, which is the planning question that comes before a commodity has an NMFC item decided, or before a shipper wants to sanity-check what a carrier's own answer should land near. It runs free in any browser, needs no licence and no login, and nothing typed in is uploaded anywhere.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is the exact NMFC item and class for this specific commodity, with its packaging rules and sub-groups?FastClass, or your carrier — that is a licensed lookup this calculator does not do.
Roughly what density-based class band should this pallet land in before I ask for a quote?This calculator — type in the dimensions, weight, and piece count, get a class estimate instantly, free, no login.
Would repacking a few inches shorter, or a few pounds heavier, earn a cheaper class on this pallet?This calculator's built-in repack levers — the height and weight it would take to reach the next class down.
How much headroom is there before a carrier's dimensioner re-rates this pallet into the class above?This calculator — the same estimate states the height at which that happens and how much clearance is left.
Does my commodity have handling, stowability, or liability rules that move it off the density-based class entirely?FastClass, or the NMFC itself — those factors are outside what a density calculator can estimate.
Do I need an account, a licence, or an install to use the tool?This calculator: no. FastClass is a licensed product sold as an ongoing subscription.

Most shippers who use both get different value from each: FastClass (or a carrier's own classification desk) for the authoritative item once a commodity is decided, and a density calculator like this one for sizing a pallet, comparing packaging options, and setting expectations before that lookup happens or before a carrier's quote comes back. This page's own estimate says as much — it is a density-based planning figure, not an NMFC classification, and it says to verify the final class with the carrier or a qualified freight professional.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or SMC³ FastClass?

They answer different questions at different points in the shipment. FastClass, from SMC³, is a licensed software product built on the official National Motor Freight Classification (NMFC) data — its job is to look up the exact NMFC item, class, and packaging rules for a known commodity, and it is sold to carriers, brokers, and shippers as an ongoing subscription. This page has no commodity database and does not look up an NMFC item at all. It estimates the density-based class band from dimensions, weight, and piece count you type in — the input FastClass needs before it can look anything up — for free, instantly, in the browser, with no login and no licence. A shipper who already knows the NMFC item for their commodity should look it up in FastClass or ask their carrier; a shipper sizing a pallet before that item is decided, or sanity-checking what a carrier's answer should land near, is in the right place here.
